description: We are a group of young and ambitious software engineers that love creating while also being able to solve real world problems.
summary:
Two NASA satellite sensors have watched Earth's fires for 25 years, but they don't count the same way. VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012) detects far more small fires than MODIS (1 km pixels, from 2000). Add the two raw records together and fire worldwide seems to jump +407% between 2011 and 2012, and +785% in Canada. That jump is the satellite changing, not the fires.

Ignis Almanac converts MODIS counts into VIIRS units with one model for the whole world, learned from the years when both sensors were flying, and joins them into one monthly record from 2001 to today. In the harmonized record the worldwide 2011 to 2012 change is +5.6%, close to the +5.2% that MODIS alone measured. Tested by hiding one year at a time, the converted monthly totals are off by 1.5% worldwide and 6.5% in Canada.

With the sensor change removed, real extremes stand out. May 2023, the start of Canada's record fire season, had 19.1 times the usual May activity. Fire managers, land managers and scientists get one baseline they can trust, for any area on Earth, for the question "is this month unusual here?"
details:
What it does: The app covers the whole world. It opens on the burning calendar, and the map is one click away.

- Pick an area: Choose one of ten preset areas (among them Canada, the Amazon, the Mediterranean, US West, Siberia, southern Africa, SE Asia, northern Australia and the whole world), type coordinates, or draw a box on the map.

- Burning calendar: The Year view shows the twelve months of one year as large tiles with the counts written in. The All years view shows every month since 2001, one row per year, with year totals and a typical-year row. A date range narrows it to the years you choose.

- Three views of the same record: Harmonized (one consistent record), Raw (MODIS and VIIRS simply added, which shows the 2012 jump), and × typical (each month against its 2003 to 2020 median).

- Three key numbers: "Is this month unusual?" compares the selected month with the same month in every other year. "When does it burn here?" shows the usual season. "Which years were worst?" ranks the years.

- Map: The selected month drawn per grid cell, with month and year pickers and a play button that steps through the months.

- Download: A CSV of hotspot counts for the search: the selected month, the selected year or the whole date range. One row per grid cell and month, with location, MODIS, VIIRS, raw and harmonized counts, and flags for estimated and provisional values.

- Method page: A technical report on the harmonization: data and cleaning, the model, validation on hidden years, approaches we tried and dropped, and limitations. It can be printed or saved as a PDF.

How the harmonization works

1. We count NASA FIRMS detections per 0.25° grid cell and month, by satellite and by day or night. We keep vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence.

2. We learn only from clean overlap years, June 2012 to 2021. The MODIS satellites' orbits drift after 2021, so later years don't represent 2000 to 2011. We drop days when any satellite was down, and we mask gas flares, which the fire data counts as vegetation fires.

3. S-NPP VIIRS is the reference sensor. From February 2012 the harmonized count is what S-NPP observed, minus gas flares.

4. Before February 2012 we convert MODIS (Terra + Aqua) into S-NPP units with one worldwide model. For each 1° block, month and day or night, it starts from a local S-NPP to MODIS ratio and applies a correction learned by gradient boosting (LightGBM) from MODIS-only inputs: how intense and how spread out the fires were, the other half of the day, the months around it and the neighboring blocks. Where MODIS saw nothing, it adds the small fires VIIRS usually finds there.

5. Before July 2002 only Terra was flying, so those months use a Terra-only version of the model.

How we checked it

- Hidden years: We hid one year of 2012 to 2021 at a time, predicted it from MODIS alone, and compared with what S-NPP really saw. Monthly error (total absolute error over all months ÷ total fire): world 1.5%, Canada 6.5%, Amazon 2.6%, Mediterranean 7.3%, US West 4.4%, Siberia 4.5%, southern Africa 2.0%, SE Asia 3.9%, northern Australia 3.3%. Yearly totals: world 0.7%, Canada 4.3%.

- Against our previous method: (per-area ratios plus a monthly power law), on the same data: world 2.1% → 1.5%, Canada 11.3% → 6.5%.

- Forward test: Fitting on 2012 to 2018 and predicting 2019 to 2021 gives similar numbers: Canada 6.7%, world 1.7%.

- Terra-only years: Hiding Aqua in 2012 to 2021 to imitate 2000 to 2002: world 2.7%, against 6.4% for the previous Terra ratio.

- The best any conversion could do: Predicting S-NPP from NOAA-20, an identical VIIRS instrument, gives 0.7% for the world and 2.5% for Canada.

- The 2012 seam: World: raw +407.2%, harmonized +5.6%, MODIS alone +5.2%. Canada: raw +785.4%, harmonized +59.8%, MODIS alone +60.5%.

- Independent audit: A separate audit engine, sharing no code with the pipeline, recomputes the Canada record built with our previous method from the raw grid and checks every published number against it (docs/AUDIT_REPORT.md).

What to keep in mind

Counts before 2012 are estimates and are marked ≈ in the app. Megafire months are the hardest: smoke hides fire from MODIS, so those months can come out 10 to 25% low. Canada and the Mediterranean stay above 5% monthly error. Outside the tested regions accuracy varies, and sparse places (the Arctic, deserts, small islands) are much less certain. 2000 to 2002 are less certain, because only Terra was flying. Months from August 2026 use near-real-time data and are marked provisional. A detection is not a fire: one large fire produces many detections.

Accessibility: A settings menu offers four colour palettes (the default fire ramp, cividis and viridis, which are colour-blind safe, and greyscale), numbers written inside the calendar cells, shapes on the status labels so colour is never the only cue, and stronger outlines. The calendar works from the keyboard and reads each cell out to screen readers. Every control has a tooltip that also appears on keyboard focus. There are light and dark themes and a phone layout.

Tools: Python (pandas, NumPy, pyarrow, DuckDB, LightGBM) for the pipeline. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the app, hosted on GitHub Pages with no build step and no server.

Public GitHub Repository: https://github.com/OM200401/SpaceApps-2026-Harmonization-MODIS-VIIRS
